notes.h: The importance of independence for older people
notes.b: Independence means an older person keeps control over daily decisions and activities, which supports dignity, health and wellbeing. It is not the same as being alone: it means choosing how to live, with support where it is needed.
points: Dignity and self-esteem: making their own decisions protects an older person's sense of worth and identity.
Physical health: staying active and managing everyday tasks maintains strength, mobility and balance, so they stay able for longer.
Mental health: making choices and having a purpose reduces the risk of depression and loneliness.
Family roles: an independent older person needs less care, so the load on family members is lighter and shared more fairly.
Living in their own home lets older people keep their routines, friends and community ties.
An older person can be independent and still accept help, such as a home support worker, because independence is about who makes the decisions.
notes.tip: Independence is the key theme: whenever you name a support or accommodation option, say what it does for the older person's independence.

notes.h: Ways older people can maintain independence at home
notes.b: Most older people want to stay in their own community for as long as they can. Small changes to the home, the right housing choice and regular contact with other people all make that possible.
points: Adapting the home: handrails, ramps, non-slip flooring, good lighting, a level-access shower, and a stairlift or downstairs bedroom, so that stairs and bathrooms stay safe. Local authority housing adaptation grants help older people and people with a disability with the cost.
Sheltered housing: self-contained units with a warden or manager on hand and shared communal facilities, so help is close without giving up a home of their own.
Bungalow living: a single-storey home removes the difficulty of stairs.
Granny flat: a self-contained unit built within or attached to a family member's house, giving privacy with family support nearby.
Downsizing to a smaller house reduces maintenance, cleaning and running costs.
Social contact: active retirement groups, community and voluntary groups, and visits from neighbours and relatives build a social circle and prevent isolation.
Meals on Wheels and similar community meal services deliver meals to the home for older people who find cooking difficult, and home support (home help) assists with everyday tasks.
Personal alarm systems let an older person call for help in an emergency while living alone, which makes living alone safer.
notes.tip: If asked for three ways to maintain independence, pick three different ones, such as adapting the home, an active retirement group and a personal alarm, and develop each in a sentence or two.

notes.h: Health and home supports available to older people
notes.b: Many older people need some help without wanting to leave home. State and voluntary supports provide that help, and each one protects a different kind of independence.
points: Home support (home help): the HSE's Home Support Service gives help with personal care and everyday tasks to people living at home, so they can stay in their own home. Home care packages exist for higher needs.
Public health nurses visit older people at home to address minor health problems and advise on care.
A medical card gives free GP visits and subsidised prescribed medicines, with a small charge per item, to people who qualify. It is granted on income (a means test) or on medical need or hardship.
The Free Travel scheme (Travel Pass) makes public transport affordable and allows older people to keep going out, which protects their social life.
The State pension gives a regular income, either contributory or non-contributory (means-tested), which supports financial independence.
Other means-tested social welfare payments provide income support to older people with insufficient means.
Voluntary and community bodies such as Age Action, ALONE, Active Retirement Ireland and Meals on Wheels groups, along with family, neighbours and friends, provide visits, shopping, meals and company.
notes.tip: When asked for supports, choose two, name each and say how it helps independence, for example a pension gives financial independence, a travel pass keeps social life going and home support allows staying at home.

notes.b: Where an older person lives affects how independent they can be and how much the family has to do. Each option has advantages and disadvantages, and the best choice differs from person to person.
points: Remaining in their own home (with adaptations and supports): advantages are familiarity, independence and community ties; disadvantages are maintenance costs, isolation and the cost of adaptations.
Living with a family member: advantages are close support and companionship; disadvantages are loss of privacy, possible generation conflict, growing dependence and strain on the carer.
Granny flat or extension: advantages are privacy with family support nearby; disadvantages are the cost of building and shared space tensions. Planning rules should be checked first.
Sheltered housing: advantages are a self-contained unit, security, contact with neighbours and a warden; disadvantages are communal rules and limited choice of location.
Residential care in a nursing home: advantages are 24-hour nursing and personal care for high needs; disadvantages are loss of the home and of independence, and high cost.
The Nursing Homes Support Scheme, known as Fair Deal and run by the HSE, helps pay for long-term care: the resident contributes according to income and assets and the HSE pays the balance.
The choice depends on health, mobility, finances, family support and, above all, the older person's own wishes.
notes.tip: When asked to discuss accommodation or grandparents living with a family, give both an advantage and a disadvantage for each option.

notes.h: Investigating accommodation options for an older relative
notes.b: A real decision about where an older relative should live is best made by gathering evidence and involving the person concerned.
points: 1. Find out the relative's health, mobility, finances and wishes by talking with them.
2. List the options, such as own home with adaptations, living with family, a granny flat, sheltered housing and a nursing home.
3. For each option, record the advantages, disadvantages and cost, including any grants or Fair Deal support.
4. Compare the options against the relative's needs and wishes, and recommend the one that keeps the most independence safely.

notes.b: Different generations grew up in different worlds, so their attitudes and expectations often clash. This is generation conflict, and it affects families at every stage.
points: Generation conflict is disagreement between members of different generations because their attitudes, values and experiences differ.
Parents and adolescents disagree over curfews, friends, technology and independence.
Adults and their own parents may disagree over care, living arrangements, spending or the older person's role in the household.
Older people may judge younger generations by their own youth without accounting for social changes such as technology and working life.
Changing moral values and lifestyle choices, such as attitudes to marriage and religion, can divide generations.
When an older person loses independence, decisions made for them can cause frustration and conflict.
notes.tip: Generation conflict is between generations, such as an adult and their own parent. Do not answer with conflict between partners. For a definition mark, say attitudes, values and experiences differ.

notes.b: Conflict between generations rarely disappears by itself. The aim is for each side to feel heard and to agree arrangements everyone can live with.
points: Good communication avoids confrontation and lets each generation state its view and listen to the other.
Clear expectations: everyone should know what is expected of them and where the boundaries lie.
Patience and understanding: recognising that values change over time reduces hostility.
Respect for experience: younger people can value the wisdom older generations have gained, and older people can accept change.
Compromise and negotiation: shared arrangements, such as visiting times or care responsibilities, are agreed together.
Early action: problems are addressed before they grow, rather than being ignored.
Regular family meetings create an atmosphere in which family members can talk openly.
Role-play practises these skills, for example a case study of an older person who resists moving into a granny flat.
notes.tip: To outline two ways of dealing with generation conflict, name each (such as communication or compromise) and say how it helps.

notes.b: Grandparents are often an important part of family life. They contribute in many ways, and the family has duties towards them in return.
points: Childcare: collecting grandchildren from school or minding them while parents work reduces childcare costs for the family.
Emotional support: grandparents listen to and reassure children and adults during stressful times.
Transmitting values: older members pass on values, traditions, culture and family history, giving children identity.
Practical help: grandparents assist with homework, meals and household maintenance.
Financial help: grandparents may help adult children with occasional costs, such as a deposit for a house.
Advice and experience: older people help with decisions and act as positive role models.
Responsibilities: respecting parents' rules and boundaries, communicating honestly and not undermining parental decisions.
As they age, the family has a duty in return to provide transport, care, company, money and emotional support to the older person.
notes.tip: When asked to discuss roles and responsibilities, cover both: give several roles, and include responsibilities such as respecting parents' decisions as well as what the family owes grandparents.

notes.b: Sharing a home brings grandparents and grandchildren closer, but it also changes family life for everyone.
points: Advantages: time with grandchildren, relaxed relationships because grandparents do not usually have to discipline, and practical help in the home.
Disadvantages: loss of privacy, differing views on child-rearing, and an extra caring burden as the grandparents age.

keyTerms.definition: Self-contained units for older people, usually with a warden or manager on hand and shared communal facilities.
A self-contained living unit built within or attached to a family member's house for an older relative.
Friction that arises when the attitudes, values or views of one generation clash with those of another.
A change to a home, such as handrails, ramps or a level-access shower, that allows a person with reduced mobility to live safely and independently.
Full-time accommodation in a nursing or care home, providing nursing and personal care for people with high care needs.
A community nurse who visits people at home to advise on health, support recovery and identify care needs.
A State entitlement giving free GP visits and certain medicines to people who meet income or health criteria.
Social and recreational groups for retired people that build friendships and reduce isolation.
The bond and interaction between members of different generations within a family.

factCards.term: Four ways older people keep their independence at home
factCards.definition: Adapting the home; using home help and home care services; receiving public health nurse visits and community meals; and using a personal alarm.
A self-contained unit of their own, a warden or manager on hand for support, and regular contact with neighbours.

factCards.term: Three disadvantages of living with a family member
factCards.definition: Loss of privacy, the risk of generation conflict, and growing dependence on the family.
Collecting them from school, minding them while parents work, and helping with homework.
Differing values and attitudes shaped by different times, and the loss of independence that can make an older person's wishes clash with family decisions.

factCards.term: Four ways to deal with generation conflict
factCards.definition: Good communication, clear boundaries and expectations, patience and understanding, and compromise through negotiation.

questions.prompt: Outline three ways in which an older person's home can be adapted to support independence.
questions.model: Any three, each with a brief explanation. Handrails and ramps make moving around safer. A level-access shower or downstairs bedroom removes the need for stairs. Non-slip flooring and good lighting reduce the risk of falls. A stairlift helps if mobility falls. A personal alarm allows the person to call for help.

questions.prompt: Discuss the role of grandparents in supporting the family, and explain how the family can deal with generation conflict.
questions.model: Grandparents: provide childcare, such as collecting children from school or minding them while parents work; give emotional support and reassurance; pass on values, traditions, culture and family history; help with homework, meals and housework; give financial help with occasional costs; offer advice and act as role models. Their responsibilities include respecting parents' rules, communicating honestly and not undermining parental decisions. Generation conflict: arises when the views of one generation clash with another, for example over childcare, living arrangements or changing values. Management: good communication that lets each side be heard; clear expectations and boundaries; patience and understanding that values change; respect for the experience of older people and the views of younger people; compromise and negotiation on shared arrangements; early action rather than ignoring problems. Full marks need roles with examples and both causes and management methods.
